articles.text: Roby Bros. and Heegaard & Hoke were burned out in Mandan, Monday morning. The loss to both firms was $15,000. Insurance, $10,750.
articles.summary: Two Mandan firms burned out Monday morning; $15,000 loss, $10,750 insured.

articles.text: The Dawes' bill for the opening of the Sioux reservation passed the Senate without a dissenting vote anp will probably pass the House easily as soon as it can be reached.
articles.summary: The Dawes bill to open the Sioux reservation passed the Senate unanimously.

articles.text: Jacob Wertheimer, proprietor of the Merchants' Hotel in Deadwood, died on January 27, of bronchitis. No one who has ever been to Deadwood was unacquainted with the genial "Jakey" and many will mourn his loss.
articles.summary: Death of Deadwood hotel proprietor Jacob Wertheimer on January 27.

articles.text: Of all the imbecile staggers at poetry that were ever perpetrated on an unoffending public, those in the railroad column of the Glendive Independent are the chief. For Heaven's sake, Widmyer, let up!
articles.summary: Packard mocks the railroad-column poetry of the Glendive Independent.

articles.text: Gladstone, after defeating Lord Salisbury the English Premier, by very doubtful means, is again forming a cabinet and will again take up the burden of government where he laid it off a few months ago. It is almost certain that Gladstone's success is due to a combination with Parnell by which Ireland is guaranteed home rule.
articles.summary: Comment on Gladstone forming a new British cabinet with Parnell's support.

articles.text: Since Theodore Roosevelt gave his lecture on ranch life, he has received about 100 applications for places on his ranch. They have come from clerks, salesmen, professional men, mechanics and laborers, and the evident desire of each one was for an opportunity to lead an easy and careless life, away from the hard work of the city. The professional men asked for superintendencies, and the clerks wanted a chance to do a little figuring, but the mechanics had but faint ideas of how they were to make themselves useful in a log or mud hut, or among the herds.—[Bismarck Tribune.
articles.summary: Clipped from the Bismarck Tribune: since his lecture on ranch life, Theodore Roosevelt has received about 100 applications for places on his ranch.

articles.text: Will the editor of the Mandan Pioneer go back to the time when the writer of this article was condemning the Mandan water-works system in the Bismarck Tribune and the editor of the Pioneer was lauding them in his paper? The total loss in Mandan's late destructive fires has caused the Pioneer to sing the same tune the Tribune sang over two years ago. It would have been a blessing to Mandan if the Pioneer had joined the Tribune in condemning what it and every citizen in Mandan recognized as a swindle, pure and simple.
articles.summary: Packard needles the Mandan Pioneer over its past praise of the Mandan water-works after the recent Mandan fires.

articles.text: We do not think there is a person in the county why has paid his tax levied by Stark county and we think more strongly than ever that a test case will show the law to be unconstitutional. Howard Eaton has secured the opinion of an able lawyer on the subject, who coincides with the authority we published last week and goes deeper into the discussion. He proves conclusively that the tax levied for school, road and bridge purposes is taxation without representation and consequently unlawful. The taxation for territorial purposes might hold if embodied in a law by itself, but coupled with the others, makes the whole law unconstitutional. Stark county will undoubtedly fight the matter and Billings will be organized none too soon to protect the interests of her citizens.
articles.summary: Packard argues the Stark county tax on Billings county residents is unconstitutional, citing a legal opinion obtained by Howard Eaton.

articles.text:
MEDORA, DAK., Feb. 1.—Some time ago a petition was circulated, asking that the county of Billings be organized. It is now affixed to Morton county for judicial purposes and is taxed seven mills on the dollar. Many oppose the organization of Billings county, because in that event, taxation would be twenty-five or thirty mills on the dollar.—[Bismarck Tribune.

What earthly object inspired the writer of the above, besides ignorance, it is hard to tell. Morton county levies no tax whatever on Billings county, much less seven mills on the dollar. If there is a solitary opponent to the organization of the county, we have yet to hear him express his opinion. There are now not more than two voters in the county who refused to sign the petition for organization, which was signed by more than 170 voters. Finally, we wish to state, that provided we receive $4,000 rail-road tax, there will never be an honest tax of twelve mills on the dollar at the present rate of assessment, except to meet some extraordinary expenditure, which must first be voted on by the people.
articles.summary: Packard rebuts a Bismarck Tribune dispatch claiming opposition to Billings county organization; says the petition had more than 170 signers.

articles.headline: At Last.
articles.text:
In another column will be found the notice for the election of county officers and a county seat for Billings county. It was a long time in coming but has now gone beyond the power of any outsider, or insider for that matter, to stop. In spite of politics, shyster lawers, wind or weather, Billings county will be organized on the second Monday in April. And now it behooves our citizens to drop entirely such log-rolling as characterized a few weeks of political discussion last fall and all unite on men who are qualified for the different offices. It should be agreed by all that in the first place, the stockmen name two of the three commissioners. This can be done by them in a caucus pre-vious to the one in which the balance of the ticket is nominated and their nominees can be approved by the mass convention or nominating caucus.

We have no especial favorites to bring forward for the different offices and provided good men are nominated will work and vote for the caucus nominees. Every man, however, who wants an honest administration of the county affairs should make up his mind that only men known to be capable and honest are nominated and elected. There is plenty of good, sound timber in Billings county ont of which to make candidates and it should be used in every case.

It will require time and trouble for every man to attend both the nominating convention and the election, but each man owes it to himself and his neighbors to take that trouble.

It might have been better to have had three polling places instead of one, but it was found impossible to define voting precincts distinctly and the governor thought it better to have only the one at Medora for the first time and to have the precincts defined before the next election.

As it is no one's duty in particular to call a nominating caucus, we suggest Monday, March 1, as a good day. We have no particular reason for naming this day except that it is far enough away to give every one notice in the county and as it is a month from the election, two trips can be arranged by some living at a distance which would be difficult if the times were nearer together. Provided there is no opposition to the day we will publish the call in our next issue.
articles.summary: Editorial announcing the election notice for organizing Billings county on the second Monday in April and urging stockmen to name two of three commissioners.

articles.text: The large purchase by Col. J. N. Simpson of Dallas, president of the Texas live-stock association, of the Goddart ranch, and 16,000 head of cattle on the Pecos, involving an expenditure of about $250,000, indicates that the colonel has faith in Texas investments. It looks, too, as though he prefers buying to leasing at six cents. The purchase was made by Col. Simpson just prior to the meeting of the cattlemen's convention in Austin.—[San Antonio Express.

articles.text: The National range convention, in session at Denver, adjourned last Saturday to meet the second Monday in February, 1887, at Denver, which will be the permanent headquarters of the association. The officers for the ensuing year are: president, Col. R. G. Head, of Colorado; secretary, J. C. Leary, of New Mexico; treasurer, Hon. J. L. Routt, of Colorado and senior vice-presiden, Thomas Sturgis, of Wyoming. Much good will follow the organization of this association as it is the first attempt by rangemen from all quarters to combine for their own protection.
articles.summary: The National range convention at Denver adjourned, electing R. G. Head president and making Denver its permanent headquarters.

articles.text: We have before had occasion to allude to the Western Rural's ideas of the range industry. The last issue especially contained a mass of twaddle that it seems scarcely possible could find a medium of publication. It says: "It is a great wrong to our breeders upon the farm to compel them to compete with those who are breeding and fattening cattle upon the people's lands without paying a penny for their use." The Rural should know, whether it does or not, that nine acres out of ten occupied by range attle are totally unfit for cultivation. In the case of the tenth acre, we defy the Rural or any other paper to show a solitary instance where there has been opposition to have it cultivated. In many cases, especially in Texas and Colorado, ranges that were formerly occupied by cattle have been entirely given over to small farmers. Moreover, ranch associations have repeatedly petitioned Congress to settle the matter of leases in some way, so that the cattleman may have some kind of a tenure to his land. As it is now no cattleman in the north has a defined range of his own and other cattle are as free to graze on his range as his own cattle are. It seems to be the universal sentiment among cattlemen, as expressed in conventions, that they wish to have some title to their ranges and that they are willing to pay for the same. The Rural article shows a dog-in-the-manger policy that shames an Indian. Eastern breeders cannot use the western ranges and consequently, according to the Rural, it is an outrage for them to be used at all. The gist of the whole article, however, is in the fact that range cattle have lowered the price of beef so that there is not as much profit in it as hitherto for eastern breeders. What do the laboring constituents of the Rural think of this? It would put down a perfectly legitimate industry that has reduced the price of beef to a point where all can use it. That is, it would compel the masses of the people to pay millions of dollars more for their beef than they do now all for the sake of a disgruntled lot of kickers who are attempting at the same time to make a living out of the very industry they are trying to crush, by selling their pedigreed and almost useless cattle to rangemen. Consistency holds no place among the jewels in the Rural diadem. And now will the Rural turn its arrows to that Congress which refuses to lease land to cattlemen who are perfectly willing to pay for the same, and put the blame, if there is any, where it belongs. As an answer to the whole phillippic of the Rural, we ask: How are the cattlemen to pay for grazing their cattle on the public domain, when the government will not receive their money and in what respect they are to blame when they have repeatedly offered to pay.
articles.summary: Packard rebuts the Western Rural's attack on range cattlemen and argues cattlemen want title to their ranges.

articles.text: The large bunch of cattle that drifted down below Dickinson have been driven back into the Bad Lands. They are not much the worse for their stay on the prairie, the steers especially being in good condition. Some of the pilgrims, however, are looking pretty thin.
articles.summary: Cattle that drifted below Dickinson have been driven back into the Bad Lands in fair condition.

articles.text: The Fargo Insurance company has adjusted and liquidated some $50,000 of losses during the year 1885. On its hail insurance business its adjusters in the field made their returns from eighteen to twenty-five bushels to the acre, subject to the approval of the board of directors. At their meeting, the final adjustment reduced the amount less than twenty-five per cent, and the paid losses average on the hail business about sixteen bushels of wheat to the acre. It is said that the production of wheat on the average in the territory was less than fifteen bushels to the acre, and this would look as though the Fargo Insurance company had been exceedingly fair in its settlement with policy holders. The officers have gone on, in a quiet yet effective way, and have met the disasters of the season's work as befitting men who have gone into the business with the determination to fulfill their obligations. They have made no special effort to attract attention, and in a quiet and and business like manner have met the demands of their patrons without a murmur. The company does not pretend that it did not lose money on the hail business during the year 1885, but having liquidated all claims against it, feels that in retiring from that branch of the insurance business it has a right to expect credit for meeting its obligations honorably and fairly, and now the Fargo proposes to push a legitimate fire insurance, and asks of the public a fair share of patronage.—[Fargo Argus.
articles.summary: Clipped from the Fargo Argus: the Fargo Insurance company settled about $50,000 of 1885 losses and is leaving hail insurance for fire insurance.

articles.headline: Roosevelt on Cowboys and Indians.
articles.text:
In a recent lecture in New York, Theodore Roosevelt gave additional evidence of his admiration for the cowboy and his contempt of the Indian. Here is an extract:

"I suppose I should be ashamed to say that I take the western view of the Indian. I don't go so far as to think that the only good Indians are the dead Indians, but I believe that nine out of every ten are and I shouldn't like to inquire too closely into the case of the tenth. The most vicious cowboy has more moral principle than the average Indian. Turn 300 low families of New York into New Jersey, support them for fifty years in vicious idleness, and you will have some idea of what the Indians are. Reckless, revengeful, fiendishly cruel, they rob and murder, not the cowboys, who can take care of themselves, but the defenseless, lone settler on the plains. As for the soldiers, an Indian chief once asked Sheridan for a cannon. "What? do you want to kill my soldiers with it?" "No," replied the chief. "Want to kill cowboy; kill soldier with a club." Ranch life is ephemeral. Fences are spreading all over the western country and by the end of the century most of it will be under cultivation. I, for one will be sorry to see it go; for when the cowboy disappears one of the best and healthiest phases of western life will disappear with him.—[Mandan Pioneer.
articles.summary: Clipped from the Mandan Pioneer: an extract from Theodore Roosevelt's recent New York lecture on cowboys, Indians and the passing of ranch life.

articles.text: Rassie Deffebach returned from the E6 ranch last Thursday evening. He reports the E6 cattle and those in Cave Hills as being in tip-top condition, better even than those in the Bad Lands. The E6 will start a horse-herd on the South Moreau, having bought out Macy's ranch, and Rassie will manage it.
articles.summary: Rassie Deffebach reports E6 and Cave Hills cattle in top condition; the E6 bought Macy's ranch to start a horse herd on the South Moreau.

articles.text: Bob Roberts will leave for Buffalo Gap and the railroad south of the Black Hills as soon as the weather moderates sufficiently. articles.summary: Bob Roberts, Dick Carr and others plan to leave about March 1 for railroad contract work on the extension to Fort Fetterman.

articles.text: Again have the merry wedding bells pealed forth and again are two hearts made happy. This time, Miss Jennie Macbeth of Mankato, Minn., and W. H. Merrifield of the Maltese cross ranch are the subjects of congratulation. Both are too well known and liked here to need any remarks except the universal wish for the happy married life which they are sure to enjoy. The marriage took place in Mankato, Tuesday night.
articles.summary: W. H. Merrifield of the Maltese Cross ranch married Miss Jennie Macbeth at Mankato, Minn., Tuesday night.

articles.text: If any further reason in favor of organization were necessary, the delay of Stark county's alleged deputy in serving his warrant on Bill Jones is sufficient. Such tardy justice is a shame and a mockery. It matters not whether the warrant was issued on account of the brutal shooting of a dog or a man, the probabilities are that there will be the same delay and subsequent failure in obtaining justice, as long as our affairs are governed by another county. We cannot be too thankful that Billings county will soon dispense her own justice.
articles.summary: Packard cites the Stark county deputy's failure to serve a warrant on Bill Jones as a reason for organizing Billings county.

articles.text: Last Saturday produced the largest number of "drunks and disorderlies" that Medora has seen for many a day. The wind-up came in the shooting of a valuable dog by Bill Jones. The dog was a large, affectionate creature, owned by Miss Helen Wade and the shooting was an outrage that cannot be sufficiently punished. A warrant was sworn out in Dickinson for Jones' arrest and a deputy came up Monday night. We are informed that he was several times in Jones' company and at least once engaged him in conversation. Tuesday morning he returned to Dickinson with the report that he could not find Jones anywhere, but that he would get him if it took until next summer. This has no other meaning than that he will make as many trips as possible so as to triple or quadruple his fees.
articles.summary: After a Saturday of drunkenness in Medora, Bill Jones shot Miss Helen Wade's dog; a Dickinson deputy came Monday night but returned Tuesday without arresting him.

articles.headline: Notice of Election.
articles.text:
Notice is hereby given that on the Second (2nd.) Monday in April, 1886, at the following place, viz.: at the town of MEDORA, in the County of Billings, an election will be held for the following officers of said county of Billings, in said Territory of Dakota, in the organization of said county;
Three County Commissioners,
One Register of Deeds,
One County Clerk,
One Sheriff,
One Assessor,
One Judge of Probate,
One County Treasurer,
One County Surveyor,
One Coroner,
One Superintendent of Public Schools,
Four Justices of the Peace,
Four Constables,
and also for the temporary location of the County seat of said county, which election will be open at the hour of eight o'clock in the morning and will continue open until five o'clock in the afternoon of the same day.
Dated this [30th?] day of January, 1886.
{Seal.} GILBERT A. PIERCE, Governor.
M. L. McCORMACK, Secretary.
articles.summary: Governor Gilbert A. Pierce's proclamation of an election at Medora on the second Monday in April 1886 to organize Billings county and locate its temporary county seat.
